text: For the choirmaster. A psalm of David.
How long, LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me?
How long must I carry worries within me, with grief in my heart all the day? How long will my enemy triumph over me?

versions.text: How long must I wrestle with my thoughts, with grief in my heart day after day? How long will my enemy triumph over me?
versions.explanation: The Hebrew idiom 'set counsels in my soul' pictures the sufferer turning plans over inside himself; 'wrestle with my thoughts' is a fairly free paraphrase. Also 'יוֹמָם' means 'by day / all day long' rather than 'day after day.' The suggested wording stays closer to the Hebrew while keeping the oral rhythm.

text: Look at me and answer, LORD my God. Give light to my eyes, or I will sleep the sleep of death,
and my enemy will say, "I have overcome him," and my foes will rejoice when I fall.
But I trust in your steadfast love; my heart rejoices in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for he has dealt bountifully with me.

versions.text: But I trust in your steadfast love; my heart rejoices in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, for he has been good to me.
versions.explanation: The verb גָּמַל carries the sense of repaying or dealing generously/bountifully, which is stronger than the general 'has been good to me.' The fuller rendering preserves the note of abundant, rewarding kindness that closes the psalm.
